title: Scientists Reveal Why Snail Shells Spiral Right‑Handed or Left‑Handed, Solving Long‑Standing Mystery
body:
A team of researchers has identified a single gene that decides whether the shell of the Japanese land snail *Euhadra quaesita* coils to the right (dextral) or to the left (sinistral), shedding new light on the genetic mechanisms that drive left‑right asymmetry in animals – a trait that also underpins the handedness of humans. The discovery, made through a combination of genetic mapping, CRISPR gene‑editing and detailed embryological studies, marks the first time a definitive “handedness gene” has been isolated in a multicellular organism and opens fresh avenues for exploring how asymmetry is established during development.

The investigation began with a long‑standing puzzle in malacology: while most snail species produce dextral shells, a minority, including certain populations of *Euhadra*, display sinistral coiling. Earlier breeding experiments hinted at a heritable factor, but the precise genetic basis remained elusive. By crossing thousands of snails with opposite coiling directions and sequencing their genomes, the scientists pinpointed a narrow region on chromosome 5 that consistently correlated with shell chirality. Within this locus they identified a previously uncharacterised gene, now dubbed **Lsd1** (for “left‑right shell determinant 1”), which encodes a protein involved in early embryonic cell‑division orientation.

To confirm Lsd1’s role, the team employed CRISPR‑Cas9 to knock out the gene in dextral embryos. Strikingly, the edited snails developed sinistral shells, while restoring a functional copy rescued the right‑coiling phenotype. Further microscopy revealed that Lsd1 influences the direction of the first cleavage spindle during the one‑cell stage, effectively setting a molecular “handedness cue” that propagates through subsequent development. This mechanism mirrors the way certain vertebrate genes, such as *NODAL* and *LEFTY*, orchestrate left‑right patterning of internal organs, suggesting a deep evolutionary conservation of asymmetry‑establishing pathways.

The implications of the find extend beyond gastropods. Human handedness—whether a person prefers the right or left hand for tasks—has long been known to have a genetic component, yet the specific genes involved have been difficult to isolate. By demonstrating that a single gene can dictate a macroscopic asymmetrical trait in a relatively simple organism, the study provides a tangible model for dissecting similar processes in more complex bodies. “Understanding how Lsd1 biases cellular orientation gives us a blueprint for how subtle molecular differences can be amplified into whole‑organism asymmetry,” said Dr. Maya Patel, a developmental biologist not involved with the work. “It bridges a gap between the genetic code and the physical manifestation of handedness.”

The research also carries practical ramifications for snail farming and biodiversity conservation. Sinistral snails are less common and often avoided by predators that have evolved to handle dextral shells, offering a potential natural defense mechanism. Knowing the genetic switch that controls coiling could enable selective breeding programs to produce snails with desired shell orientations, enhancing yields in culinary or ornamental markets. Moreover, the ability to manipulate chirality may aid in preserving rare sinistral populations that are vulnerable to habitat loss.

Looking ahead, the team plans to investigate whether Lsd1 interacts with other developmental pathways and to explore its presence in related molluscan species. Comparative studies could reveal whether similar “handedness genes” have independently arisen or share a common ancestry across the animal kingdom. As scientists continue to decode the genetic choreography behind left‑right asymmetry, the humble snail may prove to be an indispensable model for unraveling one of biology’s most enduring mysteries—how the blueprint of life translates into the handedness that shapes both shells and, ultimately, our own bodies.
